graphemes: Look up on a clear day. The sky is blue. But sunlight itself? White. So where does the blue actually come from?

graphemes: The answer is written into the air itself — tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, each one far smaller than a wave of light.

graphemes: When sunlight hits those molecules, they scatter short blue wavelengths in every direction — several times more strongly than they scatter red.

graphemes: That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from everywhere overhead. And that is why the whole sky glows blue.

graphemes: At sunset, that sunlight crosses much more air. The blue gets scattered away along the way, and the reds and oranges remain.

graphemes: Dust and pollution, on the other hand, scatter all colors equally. That is why a hazy sky looks pale and white.

graphemes: So the blue sky is not a thing. It is sunlight, rearranged by the air. Thanks for watching.
